title: {{NAME}} and the Siege of the Alabaster Palace
moral: Cleverness and kindness together are stronger than any power used alone.

pages.content:
The Alabaster Palace stood on a hill of white quartz, catching the morning light and throwing it back in every direction like an argument nobody had won yet. Its towers were slender and impossibly high, its gates were carved from a single piece of pale marble, and the mechanical sentinels that patrolled its outer walls were the finest robots ever built, or had been, until three days ago when someone had reprogrammed all of them at once.

Now the sentinels marched in the wrong direction, opened doors they were supposed to close, and had jammed every lock in the palace simultaneously. The princess was inside. Forty-seven palace staff were inside. And the only person standing outside the great marble gate, looking at it with an expression of focused irritation, was a superhero named Ord.

Ord was not what {{NAME}} had expected from a superhero. He was short, broadly built, and he dressed in deep amber with no cape on the grounds that capes, he had once explained to a journalist, were an obvious structural weakness in any combat scenario.

He had enormous hands, each capable of bending steel, and he was currently using them to hold the situation report he had just received from the palace's communications system.

'You're the code specialist?' he asked without looking up as {{NAME}} arrived.

'I solve problems,' {{NAME}} said carefully.

'Same thing,' said Ord. 'Look at this.'

pages.content:
The situation report was thorough and alarming in equal measure.

Every robot in the palace, from the massive wall sentinels down to the small dome-headed domestic units that polished the floors, had received the same overwrite at precisely midnight. The overwrite had not deleted their personalities or their original programming. It had, more cleverly, simply shuffled everything sideways. The sentinels now believed the interior of the palace was the exterior and vice versa. The domestic units were attempting to polish the quartz hill.

'Whoever did this,' Ord said, 'understood the robots deeply. You don't shuffle systems like this without knowing how they think.'

'You'd need to care about them,' {{NAME}} said slowly, thinking aloud. 'Enough to understand them. This isn't vandalism. This is.'

'What?' Ord looked at him sharply.

'A test. Or a message.' {{NAME}} looked at the nearest sentinel, tramping resolutely toward the outer wall in the direction it now believed was inward. 'Who built these robots?'

A voice came from directly above them. They both looked up.

Perched on the top of the marble gate, legs dangling, was a girl their age in a dusty workshop coat, her dark hair escaping from a complicated braid, her hands stained with grease and her expression caught somewhere between guilty and delighted.

'My mother built them,' she said. 'I'm Ven. I am also the princess. And I reprogrammed them myself, because I needed someone to come who was curious enough to ask that question instead of just hitting things.'

pages.content:
Princess Ven's actual problem was spectacular.

She dropped down from the gate and led them through a concealed side entrance she had built herself, explaining rapidly as they walked. Beneath the Alabaster Palace was a robot workshop, three floors underground, that her mother had never finished. The centrepiece of the workshop was an unfinished robot of enormous complexity, a kind the world had never seen before, intended to be not a sentinel or a servant but a collaborator, a thinking companion capable of genuine decisions.

'But the final component is stored in the vault,' Ven said, 'and the vault is sealed by the head sentinel's authentication. The head sentinel is currently trying to patrol the kitchen ceiling because it thinks the kitchen ceiling is the outer rampart.'

'And you need us to retrieve the component,' Ord said.

'I need you to reach the head sentinel without triggering its emergency protocols,' Ven said, 'which activate if any person or object over thirty kilograms approaches it while it's in override mode.' She looked at Ord's considerable frame. 'You are very much over thirty kilograms.'

Ord looked at himself. 'Yes,' he agreed.

They both looked at {{NAME}}.

{{NAME}} thought about it for three seconds, which was all that seemed necessary. 'Draw its attention,' he said to Ord. 'Something loud and safe, away from the kitchen. Give me two minutes.' He looked at Ven. 'You navigate. You know this palace.'

pages.content:
The head sentinel was enormous, three metres of bronze certainty, and it had managed to attach itself to the kitchen ceiling with magnetic foot-pads and was patrolling upside down with the dedicated focus of a machine that did not know it was upside down.

Ord's distraction worked beautifully. The sentinel's head rotated toward the sound, its emergency sensors engaged, and it began a slow upside-down march toward the far wall.

{{NAME}} and Ven had sixty seconds.

Ven led him directly to the vault, a plain steel door set into the kitchen floor. She pressed her thumb to the panel. Nothing. 'Still locked to the head sentinel's authentication,' she said tightly.

The sixty seconds were up. The sentinel's head rotated back.

{{NAME}} stepped forward and looked up at it, the great amber lenses tracking down to find him. He stood still, hands visible, nothing threatening.

'You know me,' he said. It was a gamble, the kind that felt right before you knew why. 'I've been here before. You let me in.'

The sentinel stared at him for a long, grinding moment. Its eyes flickered through amber, then gold, then amber again.

The vault clicked open.

Ven grabbed the component in both hands, and then grabbed {{NAME}}'s arm with her spare hand, and they ran while Ord brought the ceiling panelling down behind them as a barrier, roaring with the effortless pleasure of someone who has been waiting for permission to break something.

pages.content:
The collaborator robot, once the final component was installed, opened its eyes.

They were not amber or copper or any other mechanical colour. They were the soft blue of an early morning, and they blinked once, slowly, taking in the workshop in a way that seemed genuinely interested rather than simply scanning.

Ven stood before it, grease-stained and triumphant and trembling slightly, and the robot looked at her with those unhurried blue eyes and said, in a voice like the first note of a song: 'You took a long time.'

'You have no idea,' Ven said.

Ord righted all the misaligned sentinels in twenty minutes flat, which he seemed to find deeply satisfying. By evening the palace had its locks back, its corridors their correct orientation, and forty-seven extremely bewildered staff members who had spent the day being politely redirected by robots.

{{NAME}} sat on the quartz hillside as the last light left the sky, watching the Alabaster Palace resume its ordinary brilliance, and thought about Ven building a robot in the basement for years because she wanted a friend that could truly think.

The collaborator appeared beside him without sound, sat down in the grass with a motion too fluid for any machine, and looked at the sunset with evident appreciation.

{{NAME}} walked home in the dark, warm and tired, wondering what that blue-eyed robot would say to Ven tomorrow, when they had more time to talk, and the day after, and the one after that.
